full_title: REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES, PETITIONER, VS. BIENVENIDO R. TANTOCO, JR., DOMINADOR R. SANTIAGO, FERDINAND E. MARCOS, SUBSTITUTED BY HIS HEIRS, NAMELY IMELDA R. MARCOS, FERDINAND R. MARCOS, JR., IMEE MARCOS, AND IRENE MARCOS-ARANETA, IMELDA R. MARCOS, BIENVENIDO R. TANTOCO, SR., GLICERIA R. TANTOCO, SUBSTITUTED BY DOMINADOR R. SANTIAGO, AND MARIA LOURDES TANTOCO-PINEDA, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > N. Modes of Discovery (Rules 23–29)
topics: Purpose of discovery and the five modes under the Rules of Court
Sanctions for refusal to make discovery (Rule 29)
Documents withheld during discovery deemed intentionally concealed and inadmissible
Civil forfeiture of ill-gotten wealth: preponderance of evidence (E.O. No. 14-A, Sec. 3)
Rule 45 relaxed to re-assess evidence in a case of public importance
doctrine:
**Discovery** is the process by which parties gain access to facts that may support their claims or defenses. The Rules of Court provide five modes: depositions (Rules 23 and 24), written interrogatories (Rule 25), requests for admission (Rule 26), production or inspection of documents or things (Rule 27), and physical and mental examination of persons (Rule 28). Parties and their lawyers must give way to a proper request for discovery and disclose all evidentiary matters in their possession, "withholding nothing" (reiterating *Republic v. Sandiganbayan*, G.R. No. 90478). Rule 29 sanctions a party who refuses to make discovery, including **prohibiting the disobedient party from introducing the designated documents in evidence**.

**When a party is required during pre-trial or discovery to disclose all evidence supporting its assertions, it must produce such evidence; otherwise, all evidence existing but not so disclosed is considered intentionally concealed and is denied admission when formally offered** (reiterating G.R. No. 188881). This applies where the party repeatedly manifested that it had no more documents to produce and later offered undisclosed documents without a plausible explanation. Photocopies and unauthenticated documents are likewise excluded under the Best Evidence Rule.

A civil suit to recover unlawfully acquired property under RA 1379, or for restitution, reparation or damages, against the Marcoses and their associates, dummies, agents and nominees **is civil in nature and is proved by a preponderance of evidence** (E.O. No. 14-A, Sec. 3). The plaintiff's evidence must tend to prove the allegations of its complaint; evidence that requires "many leaps of logic" and inferences upon inferences reduces the allegations to speculation and warrants dismissal.
facts:
On July 21, 1987, the Republic, through the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG), filed in the Sandiganbayan a complaint for reconveyance, reversion, accounting, restitution and damages (Civil Case No. 0008, later expanded) against Ferdinand E. Marcos, Imelda R. Marcos, Bienvenido Tantoco, Sr., Gliceria R. Tantoco, Bienvenido R. Tantoco, Jr., Maria Lourdes Tantoco-Pineda and Dominador R. Santiago. It alleged that the Tantocos and Santiago acted as dummies of the Marcoses in acquiring personal and real properties and businesses, allowed The Duty-Free Shops to divert five percent of its taxes to the Nutrition Center of the Philippines (headed by Mrs. Marcos) and the Manila Seedling Bank (headed by Tantoco, Sr.), and obtained unwarranted tax and import privileges. It sought forfeiture of the sequestered properties, an accounting, and PHP 1,050,000,000.00 in damages.

In 1989 and 1991, respondents served interrogatories and motions for production and inspection of documents, which the Sandiganbayan granted; the Supreme Court upheld the grant on November 21, 1991 in G.R. No. 90478. During discovery from January 5 to July 14, 1993, the Republic produced documents marked Exhibits "A" to "LLL" and manifested that it had no more documents to produce. At pre-trial it nonetheless pre-marked Exhibits "MMM" to "QQQ-5" and again manifested it had no more; at the 2001 hearings it marked Exhibits "RRR" to "YYY"; and on March 16, 2007 it formally offered Exhibits "A" to "AAAAAAA-105," almost all of them not originals.

The Sandiganbayan first denied admission of all the exhibits under the Best Evidence Rule and for lack of authentication, then admitted only 11 (COA letters, a deed of assignment and promissory notes), and on June 3, 2009 excluded Exhibits "MMM" to "AAAAAAA" as documents not produced during discovery. The Supreme Court upheld the exclusion in G.R. No. 188881 on April 21, 2014; that ruling became final on June 22, 2015. Only the 11 exhibits and the testimonies of four witnesses remained.

On September 25, 2019, the Sandiganbayan dismissed the expanded complaint for insufficiency of evidence and later denied reconsideration. The Republic filed a Rule 45 petition. The Tantocos, Tantoco-Pineda and Santiago commented; the Marcoses did not.
issues: Whether the Sandiganbayan correctly excluded most of the Republic's documentary evidence on the grounds that the documents were not produced during discovery and violated the Best Evidence Rule.

Whether the Sandiganbayan correctly ruled that the Republic's remaining evidence was insufficient to prove the allegations of the Expanded Complaint by a preponderance of evidence, warranting its dismissal.
ruling:
**1. Yes.** Discovery enables parties to gain access to the facts and manage their claims or defenses, and allows courts to abbreviate proceedings and decongest dockets. In G.R. No. 90478, the Court held that civil trials "should not be carried on in the dark" and that parties must lay all their cards on the table, a mandate requiring the Republic and all lawyers to disclose all evidentiary matters in their possession. Rule 29 enforces this through sanctions such as expenses and attorney's fees, contempt, taking matters as established, prohibiting the introduction of designated documents in evidence, striking out pleadings or dismissing the action, and arrest.

Although the Republic did not directly refuse discovery, it presented documents it had not produced despite repeatedly manifesting that it had nothing beyond Exhibit "LLL," and "in brazen disregard of the Rules and in defiance of the Court's ruling in G.R. No. 90478" formally offered exhibits up to "AAAAAAA-105." In G.R. No. 188881, the Court treated this as intentional concealment, noting the Republic's failure to offer a plausible explanation and its lack of forthrightness, and held that evidence existing but not disclosed during pre-trial or discovery is considered intentionally concealed and denied admission when formally offered. That ruling, final since June 22, 2015, settled the admission of only 11 exhibits; the rest were excluded both for concealment and for violating the Best Evidence Rule, being photocopies or unauthenticated.

**2. Yes.** A forfeiture case is civil in nature, and E.O. No. 14-A, Sec. 3 provides that such suits may proceed independently of any criminal proceedings and may be proved by a preponderance of evidence. The plaintiff bears the burden of proof, and its evidence must tend to prove the allegations of its complaint. Factual questions are not proper in a Rule 45 petition, but **considering the importance of the case and to end a litigation begun in 1987, the Court set aside technicalities and re-assessed the evidence.** The COA letters (Exhibits "FF," "GG," "HH") merely recommended an audit or study of The Duty-Free Shops' books and were not proof of wrongdoing. The deed of assignment proved only the assignment. The promissory notes proved indebtedness but showed no connection with the alleged illegal acts. The handwriting expert identified Marcos's handwriting on letters of the Tantocos without showing its relevance; the PCGG lawyer's testimony that Philippine Eagle Mines had unpaid loans did not show the Tantocos were dummies; the bank officer admitted she did not know the beneficial owners of the trust accounts she handled; and the PCGG researcher's account of documents he came upon could not substitute for the documents themselves. Bridging these gaps would require "many leaps of logic" and inferences based on other inferences, so the allegations were reduced to speculation.
disposition: The petition was DENIED. The Sandiganbayan Decision dated September 25, 2019 in Civil Case No. 0008, dismissing the Expanded Complaint against all respondents for insufficiency of evidence, and its Resolution dated November 20, 2019 denying reconsideration, were AFFIRMED in toto.

bar_questions.q: In a civil action for sum of money, defendant X moved for production of all documents supporting plaintiff Y's complaint, and the court granted the motion. Y produced 20 documents and twice manifested that it had no more documents to produce. During trial, Y presented and formally offered 50 additional documents that had been in its files during discovery, without explaining why they were not produced. X objected. Should the 50 documents be admitted?

alac.answer: No. The 50 documents should be denied admission.
alac.legal_basis: Discovery under Rules 23 to 29 of the Rules of Court requires parties to disclose all evidentiary matters in their possession, withholding nothing, so that trials are not carried on in the dark. Rule 29 allows the court to prohibit a party who refuses to make discovery from introducing designated documents in evidence. When a party required to disclose all evidence supporting its assertions does not do so, all evidence existing but not disclosed is considered intentionally concealed and is denied admission when formally offered (Republic v. Tantoco, Jr., G.R. No. 250565, March 29, 2023, reiterating the ruling in G.R. No. 188881).
alac.application: Y was ordered to produce all supporting documents and twice represented that it had produced everything. The 50 documents were already in its files during discovery, and Y offered no explanation for withholding them. Admitting them now would reward concealment and surprise X with evidence it had no chance to prepare against, defeating the purpose of discovery.
alac.conclusion: The court should deny admission of the 50 undisclosed documents.

bar_questions.q: In another civil case, the court granted defendant D's motion for production of documents against plaintiff P. P produced every document in its possession and so manifested. Two years later, during trial, P obtained from a bank, through a subpoena duces tecum issued by the court, certified copies of bank records that P had never possessed. P immediately furnished D copies, explained how it obtained them, and offered them in evidence. D moves to exclude them as documents not produced during discovery. Should the motion be granted?

alac.answer: No. The bank records should not be excluded merely because they were not produced during discovery, since P did not conceal them.
alac.legal_basis: The exclusionary sanction applied in Republic v. Tantoco, Jr. (G.R. No. 250565, March 29, 2023), reiterating G.R. No. 188881, rests on intentional concealment: evidence existing but not disclosed by a party required to disclose all evidence supporting its assertions is considered intentionally concealed and denied admission when formally offered. The Court stressed the plaintiff's lack of forthrightness and its failure to give a plausible explanation for withholding documents it had. Rule 29 sanctions are directed at a party who refuses to make discovery.
alac.application: P disclosed everything it had during discovery. The bank records were not in its possession then and were obtained later through court process. P disclosed them to D at once and explained how it got them. There is no withholding and no lack of forthrightness, so the reason for the sanction is absent. The records remain subject to the ordinary rules on admissibility, such as authentication and the Best Evidence Rule.
alac.conclusion: The motion to exclude should be denied, because the sanction for non-disclosure in discovery is aimed at intentionally concealed evidence, not documents the party did not have.

bar_questions.q: The Republic filed a civil action in the Sandiganbayan to recover alleged ill-gotten wealth from Z, a business associate of a former President, alleging that Z acted as the President's dummy in acquiring several corporations. Z argues that the Republic must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt because the acts alleged are also crimes. The Republic's admitted evidence consists of letters of the COA Chairman recommending an audit of Z's company, promissory notes signed by Z for his companies in favor of a government bank, and the testimony of a PCGG researcher that he came upon documents on the former President's trust accounts. (a) What quantum of evidence is required? (b) Will the action prosper?

alac.answer: (a) Preponderance of evidence. (b) No. The evidence does not prove the allegations even by a preponderance.
alac.legal_basis: Under E.O. No. 14-A, Sec. 3, civil suits to recover unlawfully acquired property under RA 1379, or for restitution, reparation or damages, filed with the Sandiganbayan against the Marcoses and their associates, dummies, agents and nominees, may proceed independently of any criminal proceedings and may be proved by a preponderance of evidence. The plaintiff bears the burden of proof, and its evidence must tend to prove the allegations of the complaint. A letter recommending an audit is not proof of wrongdoing, promissory notes prove only indebtedness, and testimony about documents cannot substitute for the documents themselves (Republic v. Tantoco, Jr., G.R. No. 250565, March 29, 2023).
alac.application: (a) The action is civil, so preponderance of evidence, not proof beyond reasonable doubt, applies even if the same acts may also be crimes. (b) The COA letters merely recommend an audit and establish no wrongdoing. The promissory notes show that Z's companies borrowed money, not that Z was the President's dummy. The researcher's testimony is no substitute for the trust account documents themselves. Finding Z a dummy would require piling inference upon inference, which even the preponderance standard does not allow.
alac.conclusion: Only a preponderance of evidence is required, but the Republic's evidence is insufficient, so the complaint should be dismissed.

notes: The respondents' Comment also argued that the corporations allegedly used as conduits were not impleaded and that no preliminary investigation was conducted; the Court did not rule on these points. The exclusion of most exhibits had already been finally settled in G.R. No. 188881 (April 21, 2014, final June 22, 2015); this decision restates and applies that ruling. Bar question 2 applies the stated rationale (intentional concealment) to a situation the Court did not itself decide.
